opening: Lord, meet us gently today and always
body:
The end of Psalm 22 tells the whole story. I get so wrapped up in the first line, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” But later in the same psalm, it turns: “He has not hidden His face from him… He has heard his cry.”

It ends in victory and trust. Although Jesus was experiencing real human suffering—carrying the weight of our sin and entering into the feeling of abandonment we experience—He still says, “My God.” His Father, with whom He remains in a relationship.

Although crucified on the cross, Jesus did something extreme. He took on the full consequence of sin. He entered into the darkest human experience—separation, despair, and silence. Because of this, we can no longer say, “God doesn’t understand where I am.”

He went there.

It’s what faith sounds like when everything hurts: “My God…”

In Philippians 2:7: “Rather, He emptied Himself.”
He did not empty Himself of divinity. He emptied Himself by taking on humanity—not subtraction, but addition. Paul explains: “taking the form of a servant… being born in human likeness.”

He laid down visible glory, accepted human limitations—hunger, fatigue, pain—and entered into suffering with full obedience, even to the cross. This is fulfillment. This leads to exaltation.

But then human behavior enters.

From Matthew 26:56: “Then all the disciples left him and fled.”

Earlier, Jesus says, “My Father, if it is not possible that this cup pass without my drinking it, your will be done.” I have to read this over and over. It sounds like, “Can you take this away?” But it is not a statement of despair. It is a statement that the suffering is fully understood, and now resistance is gone.

That’s the shift:
from struggle → surrender.

Jesus has accepted the cup, fully aligned with the Father’s will—and then everyone leaves. All of them. Under pressure, they collapse. All human support is gone. Nothing is holding Him up…

Only the Father.

Human support failed—but divine purpose did not.

Judas hangs himself. His death is tied to the “field of blood.” That place represents regret, decisions you wish you could undo, and moments that feel stained.

Both involve blood. But Jesus’ death leads to redemption—it is surrender. Judas’ betrayal meets despair instead of surrender.

I think, this had to happen. But at the Last Supper, Judas was not a puppet. He made choices—greed, disillusionment, turning away. God used those choices. He did not cause them.

Then there is Peter. He denies Jesus three times. That hurts. I feel it—I feel the shame in it. But Peter does what Judas does not: he returns. He is restored. He becomes the rock—the one Christ builds on.

Then Jesus is led off to be crucified—but only after deliberate humiliation. They put a mock royal robe on Him, a fake crown, then rip it off and “dress Him in His own clothes.” They return Him to “normal,” but now beaten and weakened—as if to say, go now, face what’s coming.

Even on the cross, the chief priests say, “He saved others; he cannot save himself.” The very religious authorities—the ones who knew the Scriptures, who were supposed to recognize the Messiah, who had influence over the people—misread it in real time.

Wow.

Then:
“The tombs were opened, and many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep were raised… and coming out of the tombs after His resurrection, they went into the holy city and appeared to many.”

The tombs open at Jesus’ death—but they come out only after His resurrection. Jesus disrupts death itself. The boundary between death and life is shaken. What was closed is now open.

This is cosmic-level change.

His Passion.
